fix_commit.message: Fix a signed-integer overflow in fts5 that might occur when dealing with strategicly corrupted records. Bug [bugs:/info/2026-06-10T03:56:42Z | 2026-06-10T03:56:42Z].
fix_commit.author: dan

findings.title: Signed integer overflow in fts5IndexTombstoneRebuild via nElem*4
findings.message: In `fts5IndexTombstoneRebuild`, the 32-bit unsigned value read from a tombstone page header is cast to a signed `int`: `int nElem = (int)fts5GetU32(&pData1->p[4]);`. It is then multiplied by 4 without first checking that the result fits in a signed integer: `nSlot = MAX(nElem*4, MINSLOT);`. If a strategically corrupted FTS5 tombstone record stores a value for `nElem` greater than `INT_MAX/4` (~536,870,911), the multiplication `nElem*4` causes signed integer overflow — undefined behavior in C. The overflow can wrap around to a small or negative value, causing `nSlot>nSlotPerPage` to evaluate as false and `nOut` to remain 1 (Case 2 path). This bypasses the intended safeguard and can lead to incorrect memory allocation sizing and subsequent out-of-bounds access when processing corrupted database files.
findings.suggestion: Read nElem as `u32` instead of casting to `int`, and perform the bounds check before multiplying: check `nElem > (u32)nSlotPerPage/4` first (to avoid the overflow), then compute `nSlot = MAX(nElem*4, MINSLOT)` only in the else branch.

ground_truth.root_cause: The value read via `fts5GetU32()` is an unsigned 32-bit integer, but it is immediately cast to a signed `int`. Signed integer overflow in C is undefined behavior, so when `nElem` is large enough that `nElem*4` exceeds `INT_MAX`, the compiler is free to produce any result. In practice the value wraps, allowing an attacker-controlled field in a corrupted FTS5 database to defeat a bounds check.

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Signed integer overflow in fts5IndexTombstoneRebuild via nElem*4
